[PATH:empirical] Re-analysis of World Happiness Report and Gallup World Poll data (2005-2020) focusing on within-country top income quintile respondents, comparing the explanatory power (R² change) of perceived social network strength vs. GDP per capita in predicting subjective wellbeing. — Directly tests the hypothesis using cross-sectional survey data from high-income countries, allowing comparison of variance explained by the two predictors among the target subgroup.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal panel studies (e.g., German Socio-Economic Panel, British Household Panel Survey) examining within-person changes in subjective wellbeing as a function of changes in social network strength and income among top-quintile individuals. — Provides stronger causal inference and temporal precedence, addressing the limitation of cross-sectional designs and isolating effects among the wealthy in high-income settings.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing literature on income and social capital correlates of wellbeing, with subgroup analyses for top income quintile in high-income countries. — Synthesizes available evidence to assess whether the pattern holds across studies, accounting for methodological differences and publication bias, thereby confirming or refuting the generalizability of the hypothesis.

scope.domain: high-income nations, cross-sectional surveys, top income quintile

qualifier.geographic: high-income countries as defined by World Bank (e.g., OECD members, high-income non-OECD)

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of studies on income vs. social support as predictors of subjective wellbeing in OECD countries (e.g., from journals like Journal of Happiness Studies or Social Indicators Research). — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess whether the pattern holds across multiple datasets and methods, accounting for publication bias and effect size heterogeneity.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal panel data from the German Socio-Economic Panel (SOEP) or British Household Panel Survey (BHPS), comparing within-person changes in GDP per capita (or household income) and perceived social support as predictors of wellbeing over time. — Tests if the cross-sectional variance dominance persists when controlling for unobserved individual heterogeneity, offering stronger causal inference than simple cross-sectional surveys.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of studies on environmental quality and subjective wellbeing in developing countries (e.g., those indexed in Web of Science or Scopus with keywords 'subjective wellbeing', 'perceived environmental quality', 'air pollution', 'water pollution', 'developing countries') — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess the consistency of the hypothesized relationship across multiple contexts, controlling for GDP and health, and identifies potential confounds or moderators.

[PATH:empirical] Randomized information provision experiment in a developing country (e.g., India or Kenya) where participants receive objective air/water quality data vs. placebo, and subsequent changes in subjective wellbeing are measured, with controls for baseline GDP and health — Isolates causal impact of perceived vs. objective environmental quality on wellbeing, addressing endogeneity and measurement bias in observational studies.

[PATH:empirical] Gini coefficient and income inequality datasets (e.g., World Bank, UNU-WIDER) combined with subjective wellbeing indices (e.g., Gallup World Poll, OECD Better Life Index) — By partitioning countries into high-Gini collectivist vs. individualist clusters, one can test interaction effects: whether the relative predictive power of social support and environmental quality over wellbeing increases in high-inequality collectivist contexts, controlling for GDP.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical literature on relative deprivation, social capital, and environmental stress in collectivist cultures (e.g., work by Diener, Oishi, or Easterlin on cultural moderation of wellbeing determinants) — This body of theory predicts that in collectivist societies with high inequality, social support buffers the negative effects of inequality on wellbeing, while environmental quality becomes more salient due to shared public goods. Reviewing and meta-analyzing these studies can clarify mechanisms and boundary conditions for the hypothesis.
